claims.text: Sentry is a failure-management layer that runs alongside an LLM agent; when it detects a failure it retrieves matching lessons from an external playbook to guide recovery.
Sentry verifies, without access to task rewards, whether the agent recovered from a failure, and stores a new lesson only if the agent did recover.
In Sentry the full playbook never enters the agent's context; lessons are exposed only when a matching failure occurs.
The Sentry paper reports that failure lessons kept in the agent's context misfire when their failure is absent, and that removing them from an evolving playbook improves performance.
Sentry outperforms the strongest runtime-intervention baseline on every benchmark evaluated, by 37% on average.
Sentry outperforms the strongest context-evolution baseline by 39% on the two benchmarks where both are evaluated.
Combining Sentry with context evolution yields further gains over either alone.
Lessons learned by Sentry transfer to held-out tasks.
Controlled experiments in the Sentry paper show that exposing the full playbook to the agent lowers performance even when relevant lessons remain available on demand.
Runtime-intervention approaches act only when a failure occurs but do not learn from their repairs.
LLM agents often fail mid-task due to invalid tool calls, repeated actions, or poorly grounded reasoning.
Retrieval-based memories select lessons once at task start, before any failure occurs, and keep them in context for the whole trajectory.

Sentry's authors argue that kept in context, conditional lessons force the agent to judge at every step whether each applies, and it often judges wrong; an example lesson is 'if repeated searches return nothing relevant, broaden the query', which helps only when that failure is occurring.
ReasoningBank distills generalizable reasoning strategies from both successful and failed experiences, which the agent itself judges (via LLM-as-a-judge) without ground-truth labels.
ReasoningBank memory items have three fields: a title, a one-sentence description, and content with distilled reasoning steps or operational insights.
ReasoningBank retrieves the top-k relevant memory items by embedding-based similarity search and injects them into the agent's system instruction.
ReasoningBank consolidates new memory items into the bank with a simple addition operation, with no pruning of stale items described in the main text.
ReasoningBank reports up to 20% relative improvement in effectiveness and up to 16% fewer interaction steps than baselines on WebArena, Mind2Web and SWE-Bench-Verified.

ReasoningBank's authors say prior memory approaches store raw trajectories or only successful routines, leaving lessons from failures underexplored; raw trajectories are described as too lengthy and noisy to apply directly.
ACE (Agentic Context Engineering) boosts accuracy on the AppWorld benchmark by up to 17.1% by learning to engineer better contexts from execution feedback alone, without ground-truth labels.

ACE treats contexts as evolving playbooks that accumulate, refine and organize strategies through generation, reflection and curation, using structured incremental updates to prevent context collapse.
ACE reports +10.6% on agent benchmarks and +8.6% on finance benchmarks over strong baselines, while reducing adaptation latency and rollout cost.
Experiential Reflective Learning (ERL) builds a pool of reusable heuristics capturing effective strategies and failure modes by reflecting on single-attempt experiences.
ERL improves success rate by 7.8% over a ReAct baseline on Gaia2, and its ablations find selective retrieval is essential and heuristics transfer better than few-shot trajectory prompting.

Anthropic warns against stuffing a laundry list of edge cases into a prompt to cover every rule, and says hardcoding complex brittle prompt logic creates fragility and increases maintenance complexity over time.
